blocks.text: We now have a National AI Council, but does it represent?

MANILA, Philippines – I attended my first TWG (Technical Working Group) in Congress in February of 2025. I was there to advocate for a more human-centered approach to AI development and for more citizen representation in any kind of proposed AI governing body.

Since then there have been more TWGs, more discussions, and much more awareness of the promises and perils of AI and how it needs to be governed. It wasn’t the legislature but the president’s Executive Order No. 131 that establishes a national AI Governance framework, as well as an AI governing body.

In this piece I will focus specifically on the lack of representation in the National AI Council. This isn’t a blanket dismissal of the EO, but identifying another front on which we have to push so that we make sure that AI is developed in a way that serves us all.
The anxieties are real

For all the promises of how AI would move humanity forward, in the last two years of widespread adoption it has largely increased our anxiety, whether from the direct impacts of labor and education, or larger scale ones like the existential fears of super-powerful AI wiping out humanity or the catastrophic threat of the possibility of threat actors harnessing super-powerful AI to develop and deploy new kinds of biological or chemical weapons. We see these anxieties manifested in protests at the ASEAN over Pax Silica.

If you’re going to tell me that AI is as important as the discovery of fire or the harnessing of electricity, then we should all have a say in this conversation. My concern is who gets to participate in the conversation and the answer the EO gives.
Policy is imagining what the future should look like

In its most ideal practice, policy work is imagining what the future should look like and then crafting rules, guidelines, standards, and penalties that will guide the pursuit of the imagined future. Of course I know we don’t live in an ideal and sometimes we have to throw things together to address pressing concerns. I’m not saying that’s what this EO is, but I am hoping that this EO will lead to policy that is more inclusive.

To be fair, it starts by listing the standard principles of AI governance: “transparency and explainability, security and safety, accountability and integrity, human-centricity, fairness and equity, and sustainable development.”

Council Composition

One challenge I have when it speaks to human-centricity and equity, and especially to accountability, is that of the twelve seats on the council, eleven of them are assigned to government officials. The EO identifies the Executive Secretary as Chair, the Secretary of DEPDev as Vice-Chair, and other government agency heads as members.

I acknowledge that it’s important to have these heads of government involved. But this does not feel representative. We speak of whole-of-society, so in my ideal and imagined world, I would want this AI council to be more representative of the different sectors in our society.

This is why the twelfth, and single non-government spot feels perhaps even more frustrating. Here’s the text straight from the EO: “One (1) representative from the private sector to be appointed by the President from a list of nominees submitted by reputable business groups or associations…” What we get then is one person from the private sector and it’s quite clear it’s going to be someone who will be connected to business concerns. I think we can begin to rattle off the conglomerates or Big Tech adjacent people who might get this slot. I wouldn’t question that person’s competence, whoever it happens to be. But I would question their ability to represent all the stakeholders involved in AI development.
Other participation?

Some who would defend this might identify other language in the EO that invites participation. For example, the NAIC can invite representatives from: “other government agencies, local government units (LGUs), government-owned or -controlled corporations (GOCCs), state universities and colleges, the private sector, academe, civil society, and other relevant stakeholders to participate in its meetings as resource persons as may be necessary.”

Honestly, this feels more like hand-waving to participation than genuine participation. Being a resource person means that you can be asked or consulted. But that doesn’t mean that you have the power to enact anything. There’s also the “as may be necessary.” I’ve had the experience of sharing my expertise, submitting comments, and writing suggested language for policy. After the session and submissions you just hope for the best.
That’s not good enough if there isn’t going to be a labor voice, a civil society voice, a regional voice, an academic voice, and a range of other voices on the NAIC.

Another item in the EO that might allow for representation is this section: “Create, convene, and reorganize TWGs, determine their lead agencies, composition, and respective responsibilities, and ensure appropriate representation from government, the private sector, academe, civil society, and other relevant stakeholders, as may be necessary for the implementation of the Al Governance Framework.”
